newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan students battle police in fees protest.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan students battle police in fees protest.

text.p: Kenyan university students stoned riot police and barricaded roads near their campus on the outskirts of Nairobi at the weekend in a protest against an anticipated increase in fees, witnesses said on Sunday.
The riots on Saturday mirrored others in central Nairobi on Thursday, when battles between riot police and students at the main campus paralysed a big area of the city.
Witnesses said several students were injured in Saturday's incidents at the Kabete campus. Nearby shopkeepers barricaded their premises to deter looters.
Police fired teargas before the rioters withdrew to their residence halls. No arrests were reported.
Students say a new draft legislation for the country's universities will impose fees too high for poor students.
The student protests coincided with increasing pressure from opposition politicians for constitutional changes ahead of Kenyan elections due later this year.

The opposition has called on Kenyans to attend protest rallies in centres throughout the country on Monday -- despite warnings from President Daniel arap Moi and other government leaders that the rallies are banned.
State radio warned Kenyans on Saturday against attending Monday's outlawed rallies
The radio quoted Moi as saying that law enforcement agencies would be out in full force throughout Kenya on Monday to prevent the rallies going ahead.

Opposition groups and other bodies, including the National Council of Non-Government Organisations, demanding constitutional reforms before this year's general election say Monday's rallies will be "educational meetings" and therefore do not need police permission.

Some traders in central Nairobi have installed new security guards on their shops to deter looters. When a protest rally was broken up by riot police on May 31, many shops were looted and cars were stoned by unruly crowds.
On Friday, Moi warned against what he said was a new culture of violence in Kenya and accused the National Council of NGOs of meddling in politics and fomenting trouble.
Moi says there is no time for constitutional reforms before the presidential and parliamentary elections this year. No date has yet been set for the general election.

Despite the opposition campaign, Moi, 73, looks certain to extend his 19-year rule for five more years because of electoral rules -- which his opponents say unfairly aid the ruling party -- and deep personal and ethnic splits within an opposition that arose when one-party rule ended in 1991.
